study.title: Ezra 1 The decree of Cyrus and the return of the temple utensils
study.overview: The chapter opens with the decree of Cyrus, king of Persia, which allows the return of the Jews to Jerusalem and orders the rebuilding of the house of the LORD. The text presents this decision as fulfillment of the word of the LORD proclaimed by Jeremiah and as the fruit of a divine action that moves the spirit of the king. He then describes the response of the people, the resources provided by those who remained and, finally, the return of the sacred utensils taken to Babylon. The chapter marks the visible beginning of the restoration of worship in Jerusalem.

outline.title: The decree of Cyrus and the call to rebuild
outline.explanation: The narrator links the decree to the fulfillment of the word of the Lord and points out that God awakened the spirit of Cyrus. The king recognizes the sovereignty of the God of heaven and authorizes God's people to go up to Jerusalem to build the house of the LORD. It also determines that the residents of the places where the exiles live in helping them with voluntary goods and donations.

outline.title: The response of leaders and material support
outline.explanation: The chiefs of Judah and Benjamin, priests, Levites, and all who had the spirit awake by God rise up to go up and rebuild the temple. The neighbors strengthen them with silver, gold, goods, animals and other voluntary offerings, showing that restoration occurs not only by political decision, but by spiritual and community mobilization.

outline.title: Returning temple utensils
outline.explanation: Cyrus returns the utensils of the house of the LORD which Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem and placed in the house of his gods. They are handed over to Shesbazar, the prince of Judah, and carried with those who return from the captivity. The final list highlights the value and holiness of these objects, ending the chapter with the image of the restoration of the ongoing cult.

study.context: The text places the events in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, after the fall of Babylon. The notes indicate that this corresponds to the period in which the Persian empire came to dominate the region and allowed the return of exiled peoples to their lands. The chapter also relates to the prophetic promise of restoration after the period of exile, especially the word of Jeremiah. The later use of the expression "God of the Heavens" is consistent with the language of the books written after captivity, according to Adam Clarke.
study.theology: The chapter highlights God's sovereignty over kings and empires: it is the LORD who awakens the spirit of Cyrus and leads history to fulfill his word. Even a pagan ruler can be used as an instrument of the divine will, even though his political motives are not pure. Also appears the faithfulness of God to his covenant: the return of the people, the rebuilding of the temple and the return of the utensils show that the exile did not annul the promises. Moreover, the text values the obedient human response: leaders, priests, Levites and the rest of the people cooperate with readiness, and restoration involves both divine action and practical responsibility of the people. The return of the sacred utensils reinforces that the worship of the LORD is not trivial; the objects of the temple belong to the holy service and are treated as precious.

scholarViews.insight: Tyndale notes that the chapter begins as a direct continuation of the end of 2 Chronicles, showing the link between the judgment of exile and the promised restoration. He points out that God moved Cyrus' heart and used this king to publish the decree that begins the return.

Matthew Henry points out that the leaders of Judah and Benjamin, along with priests and Levites, were the first to be willing to go up to Jerusalem. To him, this teaches that in a good work, ministers and leaders must go ahead.

Adam Clarke draws attention to the final sum of the utensils, noting a difference between the detailed list and the total presented. He understands that the passage is brief and possibly summarized, but emphasizes the careful return of the consecrated vessels.

questions: What does the text teach about how God can use rulers who do not worship him to fulfill his purposes?
How does the willingness of leaders to go first confronts our tendency to expect others to take the initiative?
What goods, abilities, abilities or resources can God ask me to put at the service of the restoration of his work today?
study.practice: This chapter calls us to trust that God remains sovereign over authorities, crises and historical changes. The practical application is to respond promptly when God opens doors to serve, rebuild and restore. This may mean supporting a local work, participating in a spiritual resumption, or returning to the Lord what has been separated to him with fidelity and reverence. We are also challenged to help concretely those who are resuming the walk, not only with words, but with resources, time and encouragement.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not detail the exact date of the decree beyond the first year of Cyrus, nor fully clarify Sesbazar's historical identity beyond the title presented in the text. There is also a numerical discrepancy between the list of objects in verses 9-10 and the total of verse 11; the notes suggest that the list is summarized or that there is textual variation, but do not allow to solve the exact total without resorting to other sources.
